\begin{proof}
Let $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1$. We prove irreducibility by viewing $f$ in $\mathbb{Q}(y)[x]$. Its discriminant is
\[
\Delta=4(1-y^2)=4(1-y)(1+y).
\]
Suppose, for contradiction, that $\Delta$ were a square in $\mathbb{Q}(y)$. Writing such a square as $(a/b)^2$ with coprime $a,b\in\mathbb{Q}[y]$ would force every irreducible factor of $4(1-y)(1+y)$ to occur with even multiplicity. But $1-y$ and $1+y$ are distinct irreducible factors, each occurring once. Hence $\Delta$ is not a square.

Therefore the quadratic $f\in\mathbb{Q}(y)[x]$ is irreducible. Any nontrivial factorization in $\mathbb{Q}[x,y]$ would remain a nontrivial factorization after passing to $\mathbb{Q}(y)[x]$, which is impossible. Hence $x^2+y^2-1$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[x,y]$.\end{proof}
